topic: The Toeplitz's Conjecture: The Inscribed Square Problem
target_audience: Undergraduate students in mathematics or computer science

outline.topic: The Toeplitz's Conjecture: The Inscribed Square Problem
outline.target_audience: Undergraduate students in mathematics or computer science

sections.title: Introduction: The Intuitive Hook
sections.content: Introduce the central question: Can we always find four points on any closed loop (like a rubber band) that form a square? Define 'closed loop' as a Jordan curve in a 2D plane.
sections.example: Visualize a messy, tangled rubber band lying on a table. Can you pick four points on it that connect to form a perfect square?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Continuity and Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
sections.content: Briefly explain the role of continuity in topology. If we move along a curve, properties change smoothly. IVT ensures that if a function goes from negative to positive, it must hit zero.
sections.example: Imagine a hiker climbing a mountain and coming down; there must be a point where the altitude is exactly equal to the starting point.

sections.title: The Configuration Space Approach
sections.content: Explain how we map pairs of points on the curve. By identifying pairs of points (x, y) that represent chords, we transform the physical geometry problem into a topological intersection problem in higher dimensions.
sections.example: Represent the curve as a circle. The set of all pairs of points on this curve forms a square (topological square) or a torus-like shape.

sections.title: The Mathematical Proof Logic
sections.content: Demonstrate how the 'inscribed square' existence is equivalent to finding an intersection between a specific diagonal and the 'diagonal' of the configuration space. Use a symmetry argument: if we reflect the points, the signs flip, forcing an intersection at the origin.
sections.example: Use an animation showing a square rotating and expanding inside an irregular 'amoeba-shaped' blob until the vertices hit the boundary.

sections.title: Conclusion and Open Questions
sections.content: Summarize that for smooth curves, the square exists. Briefly mention the 'Inscribed Rectangle' case (easier, proven) vs the 'Inscribed Square' conjecture for general curves (still an active area for non-smooth curves).
sections.example: A robot arm attempting to place four markers on an arbitrary track; the math guarantees the markers can be placed as a perfect square.
